transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Rivera (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (PulseWare Head of MLOps), Sofia Lin (Platform), Raj Mehta (CTO), Anita Gomez (SRE)

Summary: quick technical deep dive following repeated CUDA OOM spikes observed in PulseWare staging cluster when serving their large instruction-tuned model in mixed precision. Focus on root cause: dynamic allocation spikes triggered by KV cache handling + prefetch + quantization fallback path; discuss mitigation: eviction tuning, prefetch backpressure, retry semantics, and a proposed on-prem smoke test in their VPC.

Topics: runtime memory spikes; KV cache growth across concurrent sessions; prefetch/async stream race; mixed precision (FP16) quantized kernel fallbacks; CANARY/retry policy; VPC MTU/timeouts (brief)

Action items (recap): see metadata above

Transcript body:
[00:00:10] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a focused triage on the staging OOMs you hit last week, and i think jonas pulled traces, so i'll hand it off to him in a sec.
[00:00:22] Jonas Rivera: yeah hi, morning e-- or afternoon depending, i'll try to keep this high signal. i've loaded the nsys capture from 09-28, there's a pattern where at t+~220s into a long-running stream we see a sudden alloc spike that exhausts device memory, it correlates to an asynchronous prefetch that fires during a lazy-kv-pop.
[00:00:45] Speaker 1: (yeah)
[00:00:48] Sofia Lin: sorry quick context, this was the 8k-instruction model, serving multi-turn chat, we normally have per-session KV caching to avoid repeated prefix compute. average batch size is 1-2 in prod, but in staging we had a short burst of concurrent sessions up to 48.
[00:01:10] Jonas Rivera: gotcha, so two stressors: many concurrent sessions each with KV cache entries, and our runtime prefetch kicking off more memory usage. importantly your quantization profile had mixed-mode fallbacks enabled for the last-layer attention kernels, so in a few traces i see a kernel path that expands to full FP32 temporaries.
[00:01:33] Raj Mehta: when you say 'expands', do you mean it reallocs on device or does it create host staging buffers?
[00:01:39] Jonas Rivera: primarily device, it's an internal expand for numerically stable attention - it's rare but when the quantized kernel detects saturation it falls back and allocs a slightly larger temp buffer, that plus concurrent KV growth is the tipping point.
[00:01:55] Evan Brooks: we also saw a handful of cudaLaunchTimeout errors in the pod logs, are those consequential or just side effects?
[00:02:02] Jonas Rivera: they're symptomatic. once memory pressure rises, kernels take longer to schedule, the watchdog kicks in on some of your nodes (drivers configured with watchdog on), and that surfaces as launch timeout. sometimes the driver resets and pod restarts.
[00:02:18] Anita Gomez: for our on-prem setup, we've got a fairly tight device memory footprint per model since nodes are 80GB A100s but we host multiple partitions, so headroom is limited. any small temp bump kills the slot.
[00:02:34] Maya Patel: ok let's enumer- enumerate mitigations, short term and medium term, and then match on test plan. jonas?
[00:02:41] Jonas Rivera: short term: 1) disable the fallback-to-fp32 path for the attention kernel on the model variant you're running in staging — you accept a tiny numerical degradation but avoid the sudden temp allocs. 2) tune KV cache eviction policy to cap per-session memory (LRU window + max-entries per-session). 3) set a conservative prefetch window so async prefetch doesn't allocate across too many pending sessions.
[00:03:08] Sofia Lin: is that something we can change via model config or does it require a runtime rebuild?
[00:03:13] Jonas Rivera: model config toggles exist for quantization fallbacks and prefetch window on our runtime; eviction policy is adjustable via route/session config, no rebuild.
[00:03:22] Speaker 2: (cool)
[00:03:25] Raj Mehta: any impact to latency if we cap cache more aggressively? our p99 is already at 320ms and we can't go above 400ms.
[00:03:33] Jonas Rivera: small regressions for cold prompts, so you might see a delta on first-turn. but for long conversation flows, capping per-session KV growth should reduce tail amplification and actually improve p99 overall because you avoid GC/eviction churn and driver resets.
[00:03:49] Evan Brooks: tell me more about the prefetch backpressure, i've seen our staging runtime spawn a lot of cudaMemcpyAsync calls then they hang, is that what you're calling prefetch?
[00:03:59] Jonas Rivera: yes, our prefetch uses separate CUDA streams to warm up weights/cache, but without backpressure it can pile up requests and create many outstanding device allocations. We recommend a semaphore-driven backpressure: limit concurrent prefetches per GPU and coordinate with batching windows so prefetches are canceled if the session goes idle.
[00:04:19] Anita Gomez: semaphores in userland, or something Redwood runtime does?
[00:04:22] Jonas Rivera: runtime-level knob. i'll attach the snippet later.
[00:04:26] Sofia Lin: you mentioned MTU and VPC timeouts earlier in the invite — did that play any part?
[00:04:31] Maya Patel: quick note: there was a side case where large embedding uploads across your VPC hit fragmentation and TCP retransmits, that increased latency for model fetches and made time windows tighter, but it's secondary to the device mem cause.
[00:04:45] Raj Mehta: ok so what about retries — if a request hits an OOM should the route retry on a different model variant automatically? we want retries to be safe and not double-charge or duplicate downstream side-effects.
[00:04:57] Jonas Rivera: we have idempotent retry semantics baked in the platform: two modes — fast-fail vs safe-retry. Safe-retry will re-route to a compatible model variant (e.g., lower-quant or smaller context) and tag the response as retried, and has a single automatic attempt. For side-effecting ops you can opt out or use provided request-idempotency headers so backends dedupe.
[00:05:21] Evan Brooks: do retries spin up new GPUs or reuse existing ones?
[00:05:24] Jonas Rivera: routing tries to reuse active capacity first; if capacity exhausted it will pick a different compatible pool or fallback to dedicated small-instance variant. it won't immediately spin up capacity in the middle of a synchronous request — that's an async fallback.
[00:05:36] Maya Patel: question from the seat, how should we calibrate the canary window for a model that has these rare fallbacks?
[00:05:43] Jonas Rivera: recommend longer canaries for quantized variants — e.g., 24-48h with synthetic load that mimics your multi-turn long sessions plus burst concurrency. Also include stress tests that force worst-case KV growth so you exercise eviction and prefetch paths.
[00:06:00] Speaker 3: (mhm)
[00:06:05] Sofia Lin: we'd like to avoid disabling fallback if possible, can you suggest thresholds where fallback is safe?
[00:06:12] Jonas Rivera: yes, two thresholds: a per-GPU outstanding-temp-memory budget (say 10% of free mem) and a per-session KV budget. if both are below thresholds allow fallback; if not, return deterministic error or route to a smaller model. We can instrument these thresholds into the runtime so it short-circuits fallback rather than letting it allocate then fail.
[00:06:33] Raj Mehta: is there instrumentation we can expose to our SRE dashboards to alert before driver watchdog fires?
[00:06:38] Jonas Rivera: yes, expose metrics: outstanding_async_prefetch_count, kv_cache_bytes_per_gpu, quant_fallback_count, device_free_memory_low_watermark. we can push a prometheus exporter config for your staging cluster.
[00:06:52] Evan Brooks: that would be great, we had no visibility into the moment before the reset.
[00:06:56] Maya Patel: jonas, did you see anything in the nsys about memory fragmentation causing failure to allocate a contiguous blob?
[00:07:03] Jonas Rivera: slightly, there were small signs of fragmentation after many ephemeral allocations. a mitigation is to prefer pooled allocators or to pin larger scratch buffers at init time for attention temps so you avoid repeated alloc/free churn. our runtime supports a scratch pool toggle.
[00:07:20] Anita Gomez: ok so immediate playbook: change route configs to cap KV per-session, set prefetch to conservative, enable scratch pool; if still spikes then disable fp32 fallback.
[00:07:29] Maya Patel: yes and i'll send the specific route snippets.
[00:07:33] Speaker 4: (inaudible)
[00:07:38] Raj Mehta: what about memory accounting for multi-tenant nodes — our operators want to run several models on same physical GPU with partitioning, how safe is that?
[00:07:47] Jonas Rivera: memory accounting is per-runtime-instance; for multi-tenant partitions we recommend explicit capacity reservations and keras-like cgroups for GPUs, couple that with runtime per-route memory caps. otherwise kernel fallback of one tenant can impact others.
[00:08:05] Sofia Lin: how often do you see quantized kernels trigger fallback in production?
[00:08:09] Jonas Rivera: for well-calibrated quant profiles it's rare, <0.1% of requests, but when it happens it's high-impact. the probability increases when you have long context windows and certain attention patterns (very peaky logits).
[00:08:23] Maya Patel: ok let's go into the trace clip that jonas highlighted, jonas you want to share screen?
[00:08:29] Jonas Rivera: sharing now — you'll see at 00:03:40 the prefetch schedule kicks off across streams 3 and 4, an async memcpy, then at 00:03:42 multiple lazy-kv-pop callbacks try to pin new entries, device alloc fails at 00:03:43, but the kernel was already queued so watchdog complains. note the quant fallback path alloc call just prior.
[00:08:54] Evan Brooks: can you replay the part where it falls back? i missed the exact call stack.
[00:08:58] Jonas Rivera: it's a small code path: check numerical range -> if failure -> lock -> allocate temp_fp32 -> convert -> run attention_fp32. the allocate is the culprit in pressure.
[00:09:11] Speaker 1: (right)
[00:09:14] Raj Mehta: question — could converting to int8 or using a different kernel avoid this?
[00:09:20] Jonas Rivera: int8 reduces memory but increases compute and can increase peak temps depending on implementation; also int8 fallbacks are more invasive. the pragmatic approach is to tune thresholds or use smaller context model variant for the most memory-sensitive routes.
[00:09:34] Sophia Lin: we run a small batch pipeline to amortize overhead, would increasing batch size help?
[00:09:40] Jonas Rivera: careful — larger batches allocate larger per-token KV and may increase temporary buffer needs; if batching increases token parallelism you could see higher transient usage. sometimes batching helps amortize kernel launch overhead but it's a tradeoff.
[00:09:55] Maya Patel: let's talk about recovery semantics — if device reset occurs are you ok with automatic retry?
[00:10:01] Evan Brooks: we prefer correlation ids and dedupe rather than blind retry, otherwise downstream systems e.g. event logs mis-record.
[00:10:08] Jonas Rivera: agreed. our safe-retry uses idempotency header; if absent we default to fast-fail and surface error to caller. We can add a flag to enable an orchestrated retry with dedupe token for your routes.
[00:10:21] Anita Gomez: fine, we'll add the idempotency header for state-changing ops.
[00:10:25] Maya Patel: moving on, jonas you mentioned a smoke test in their VPC, what's required from pulseware side?
[00:10:32] Jonas Rivera: minimal: a staging VPC endpoint we can reach (peered), sample model checkpoints or registry pointer, test harness that can replay your real request mix (we need multi-turn traces), and permission to run synthetic bursts up to 60 concurrent sessions for 30m.
[00:10:50] Evan Brooks: we can provide replay traces and a peered VPC in staging. operator will create temporary security rules.
[00:10:56] Raj Mehta: are there any secrets to share? we'll keep everything on internal network, no external model fetch.
[00:11:01] Jonas Rivera: fine, also we'll deploy a lightweight prometheus exporter to collect metrics i listed earlier.
[00:11:06] Speaker 2: (cool)
[00:11:10] Sofia Lin: one more operational Q: driver versions — does Redwood recommend a specific Nvidia driver or CUDA runtime? we've seen driver resets tied to older drivers.
[00:11:18] Jonas Rivera: yes we recommend container runtime with NVIDIA driver 525+ and CUDA 12.x for best kernel stability; older stacks have known fragmentation and driver watchdog quirks. We'll send a short compatibility matrix.
[00:11:31] Maya Patel: ok great, to summarize: immediate config changes (kv cap, prefetch conservative, enable scratch pool), instrument prometheus metrics, run canary/test in staged VPC, if still hitting spikes then toggle off quant fallback for that variant while we iterate.
[00:11:46] Evan Brooks: timeline wise we can have our replay traces and staging peering by Monday.
[00:11:51] Maya Patel: perfect. question queue open, anyone else?
[00:11:56] Anita Gomez: small nit — can you provide the exact route snippet for capping KV? we've had trouble translating examples into our helm values.
[00:12:04] Jonas Rivera: i'll paste the route snippet in the follow-up, it's a few lines: session.kv.max_entries: 1024, session.kv.max_bytes: 1GB, prefetch.concurrent_limit: 4, scratch_pool.enabled: true.
[00:12:20] Sofia Lin: thanks, that helps.
[00:12:24] Raj Mehta: one more — how do we measure the cost impact of disabling fallback? finance will ask.
[00:12:29] Maya Patel: we'll run A/B during canary and provide token-level cost delta, also Redwood Optimize can simulate cost per token for the two profiles, we'll include that.
[00:12:40] Evan Brooks: fine.
[00:12:42] Maya Patel: any final comments? otherwise we'll wrap and share notes.
[00:12:47] Raj Mehta: just appreciation, this is moving quickly. we'll action items and schedule smoke test.
[00:12:53] Maya Patel: thanks all, jonas you'll send traces and snippet, i'll send retry docs and canary suggestions.
[00:12:59] Jonas Rivera: noted.
[00:13:02] Maya Patel: cool, meeting end.
